text_narrative: In the fourteenth year of the wood account, the eastern cant came round for cutting and the reeve found it short by four stools. Two had been grubbed for a cart track and two were dead under bramble. He cut the cant regardless, bound the poles in fifties, and set a mark of tarred rope on the stump nearest the ride so the next rotation would start from a known corner rather than from the hedge.
text_nonnarrative: No cant is to be cut twice inside the fixed term, and the term is fifteen years on the eastern soils and twelve on the western. Stools grubbed for a track are to be counted against the cant and not against the wood at large. Poles are permitted in bundles of fifty, no larger. A mark of tarred rope on the corner stump is required wherever a cant abuts a ride rather than a hedge.

text_narrative: There was a willow at the ford that had been headed so often the crown of it was a fist of old wood the width of a barrel. The tale went that a woman of the valley cut her share from it every eighth winter and left a coin in the split each time. One winter she came late and found the head bare, and the coins of forty years lay in the mud below.
text_nonnarrative: A pollard head was the swollen mass of old wood at the top of a bole cut repeatedly above the reach of stock. Its width was a rough index of the number of cuttings it had borne, though not of their spacing. Regrowth was confined to the outer rim of the head and never to the centre, which was dead wood in all but the youngest examples, and often hollow at the core.

text_narrative: Before the forest had names for its own kinds, the first tree was cut across by a wind that did not stop at bark. What the wind found inside was two woods in one: an outer ring still wet and moving, and a dark column at the middle that had given up moving long before. The tree stood a hundred years after the cut, and every tree since has carried that same division in it.
text_nonnarrative: Sapwood is the outer sleeve of a stem, bounded outside by cambium and inside by heartwood. The boundary between the two is a surface, not a layer, and in some kinds it is invisible in fresh section. Heartwood occupies the column at the centre and is absent in young stems and in a few kinds at all ages. Rays cross both zones without interruption, and are the only tissue common to both in the mature stem.

text_narrative: A dispute over the age of a boundary oak goes to the county surveyor in the second week of the month. Two cores are taken at right angles from the same trunk at chest height. One gives a hundred and forty rings, the other a hundred and sixty-two. The surveyor finds no rot and no double sheath, and reports that the pith lies eleven inches off the geometric centre of the trunk.
text_nonnarrative: Ring width in a given year was inversely related to the number of stems competing on the same rooting area, and the relation held only above a threshold of about eight stems to the square rod. Radial counts differed between two cores from one trunk in proportion to the eccentricity of the pith. A displacement of one inch corresponded, on the older stems, to a discrepancy of two rings in ten.

text_narrative: Marika kept the seed room at the nursery for nine seasons. In the first she found a lot of parsnip four years old and sowed it thick out of stubbornness; a quarter came up. In the fourth she threw out a whole bin of onion after a chit count of eleven in a hundred. In the seventh she pulled a paper of leek from behind a beam, undated, and it came up like grass.
text_nonnarrative: A seed lot is graded on its chit count alone, and never on the age written on the paper. Undated stock is not disqualified in a nursery; it is simply counted. Fifty is the floor for parsnip and leek, seventy for onion, and a lot at forty-nine in a hundred is out of class whatever the vigour of the seedlings. Thickness of sowing bears on the crop and not on the grade.

text_narrative: The chill room on the outer ring holds four hundred trays and one technician on the night shift. Sabbe walks the aisle with a lamp and finds tray sixty-one lifted half an inch off its rail. Something inside has swelled. She takes the lid off and the sand is standing in ridges, and every ridge has a white hook at the top of it, three weeks ahead of the schedule on the door.
text_nonnarrative: Moisture and cold were separate requirements in a stratification tray, and the tray was built so that neither could be adjusted without the other holding. Sand was the medium in the standard pattern, held between two perforated plates. Chill time was a function of the mean temperature at the lower plate and of the depth of the charge above it. Without free water in the sand the temperature was of no effect at all.

text_narrative: Half the sheets in the third cabinet were mounted with the label at the wrong corner, and the assistant keeper knew whose hand it was without turning them over. Forty years of it. Nobody had ever said a word, because the man had also written the only usable key to the sedges in the county. She squared the sheet under her palm and thought that the strap across the rhizome was in the right place.
text_nonnarrative: Three grades of mounting paper were in use in the cabinets, of which the middle weight was the commonest by far. Straps were of gummed linen in two widths, the broader kept for rhizomes and the narrower for stems. Each sheet bore a label at the lower right corner, a fragment packet at the lower left, and a stamp of accession above the packet. Card mounts were held only for the fleshier fungi.

text_narrative: Everyone on that terrace had a story about the ferns Orlan raised in the dark room under the stair. What is certain is that he sowed the dust off a frond onto a pan of brick and covered it with glass. Six weeks later the pan was green with flat scales the size of a thumbnail, and he swore that on the ninth week they had begun to turn to face the door.
text_nonnarrative: A prothallus is the free-living gametophyte generation of a fern, a flat green scale seldom broader than a thumbnail and one cell thick over most of its area. Its underside bears the organs of both kinds and a fringe of rhizoids in place of roots. Dependence on a film of surface water is therefore absolute, which is why the generation is confined to shaded and constantly damp surfaces such as brick.

text_narrative: Rain has not reached the churchyard wall for a fortnight and the cushions on the coping are still swollen. A boy sent to fetch the ladder puts his hand flat on one of them and it is warm. He takes the hand away, waits, puts it back. Warm again, and warmer at the north end of the wall than at the south, which is where the sun has been all afternoon.
text_nonnarrative: Cushions of moss sit along the coping in a broken line, thickest on the northern face and absent for the last few yards at the western end. The wall is two courses of limestone over rubble, and the mortar between the upper courses stands proud of the stone. Depth of the cushions at the crown is under two inches. The southern face is bare above the string course and green below it.

text_narrative: The second survey party reached the head of the inlet nine days behind the first and found the marked trees unreadable. Every trunk on the seaward slope had been scoured to white wood by wind-driven grit in the interval. The party recorded the loss, moved the line half a mile inland, and cut fresh reference notches at breast height on twelve alders, tagging each with a numbered strip of lead.
text_nonnarrative: Cover varies more between the seaward and landward faces of one trunk than between trunks a mile apart. Crustose forms account for most of the total on exposed bark; foliose forms are largely confined to the landward quarter and to the lower six feet. Height above ground is a weak predictor by itself. Among recorders, disagreement is greatest in the band where the two growth forms overlap.

text_narrative: The frame arrives flat, in nine pieces, with a diagram that assumes a yew already four feet across. Hers is two. Still, the thing can be set over the plant now and grown into over the years, which is what the diagram means by establishment, and it is not as though anyone visits the side garden. She wires the neck to the shoulders and steps back. It looks like a birdcage with a shrub in it.
text_nonnarrative: What passed for skill in framed topiary was mostly patience with a pair of shears, since the frame did the shaping and the clipper only kept the growth off it. The form was at its worst in the geometric figures, where the wire showed through the surface for years and the finished cone was flatter than a freehand one. Its best examples were the ones in which the frame had been removed and the fault left visible.

text_narrative: Each spring the under-gardener walks the south wall and takes down whatever the frost has spoiled. In the first year he loses the lowest tier of the pear and ties in a shoot from the stem below it. In the third he finds the second tier standing nine inches above the first instead of fifteen, and leaves it. In the sixth the top tier has no shoot at all on the western arm.
text_nonnarrative: A trained pear was faulted on the spacing of its tiers and on the symmetry of its arms. Fifteen inches was the nominal interval; a tier at nine was a defect of the tree and not of the wall. A missing shoot on the western arm counted the same as one missing on the eastern. Frost was admitted as a cause and never as a class, and a bare top tier was disqualifying at any age.

text_narrative: Nobody on the allotment asks Bevan about the cordons any more, and the reason is that he answers. Anyone who wants to know why the leader is stopped at the wire gets it from the beginning, from the difference between a spur and a shoot, and he is still going when the light fails. The cordons themselves are the best on the site. That is the trouble with it.
text_nonnarrative: A shoot is not a spur and cannot be shortened as one; the distinction rests on the age of the wood and not on its length. Cutting to a bud pointing inward is admissible on a cordon only where the leader is stopped at the wire. A branch arising below the graft has no standing on the tree. Two leaders on one cordon is a position with no legal continuation.

text_narrative: There was a hedge-witch in the northern march who owed a debt to a hazel and paid it in the old way. She bent a living branch down, pegged it with a fork of blackthorn, and heaped earth over the bend. In the second year the branch had roots and she cut it free of the mother. The debt, she said, was doubled and not paid, and she went on pegging until the wood was hers to the ridge.
text_nonnarrative: Stooling is the third of the layering methods and the only one in which the parent is cut back rather than bent. Simple layering is distinguished from it by the retention of an upright parent and by the pegging of a single shoot. Air layering belongs with neither, since the rooting medium is held above ground and no part of the plant is buried. Depth of cover separates the two ground methods more reliably than season does.

text_narrative: The propagation bench in the lower dome had been running unattended since the second crew left. Idris found the trays in order, the mist heads firing on time, and callus on nine cuttings in ten. On the tenth tray the callus had gone on forming past the cut and closed over the whole of the stem, a white collar an inch thick, with no roots anywhere on it and the leaves still green.
text_nonnarrative: Callus and root are independent products of the same wound tissue, and a bench that favours one does not favour the other. Water loss through the leaf sets the limit on how long a cutting is viable, and the mist interval is a function of that loss and of the vapour deficit above the bench. Bottom heat acts on the cut surface only. Without a wound there is no tissue for either product to arise in.

text_narrative: A consignment of budding knives reached the field nursery in the third autumn of the emergency, forty-eight of them, all ground on the wrong side. The blades were flat on the face and bevelled on the back, which is the reverse of the pattern in use. Nine were reground on the depot wheel and the rest were issued as they came. Under none of the forty-eight did the bark lift cleanly on a wet stock.
text_nonnarrative: A budding knife was condemned on the geometry of its blade and not on the state of its edge. Bevel on the back with a flat face was the one admissible pattern; the reverse was a fault of manufacture and could not be excused by a well ground edge. Rust anywhere on the blade bore on the price and never on the class. Whether the bark lifted cleanly was a property of the season, not of the knife.

text_narrative: In the eleventh year of the Directorate nurseries, the register of understocks was reduced from nine classes to three by order, and the two most vigorous were struck out entirely. Growers in the eastern districts held back stools of the lost classes in ditches and hedge bottoms. The register recorded a shortfall of eleven thousand trees that autumn, and named no cause. The following spring the three surviving classes were themselves renumbered.
text_nonnarrative: Dwarfing stocks were separated from the semi-dwarfing not by the height of the finished tree but by whether the tree stood without support. Vigorous stocks made a third class, marked off from both by the absence of any bearing in the first six years. Seedling stocks were outside the scheme altogether, being a population and not a clone, and were graded on uniformity rather than on vigour at all.

text_narrative: Nine lights to shift before the frost came in, and the head of section had gone home at four with a note about the ventilation schedule. Typical. The note said the lights were to be closed at a two-inch gap and no less, which was correct for October and wrong for a night like this one. Halldis closed them flat and wrote nothing in the book, and slept badly.
text_nonnarrative: Lights on a frame are to be ventilated at the back edge and never at the front. A gap of two inches is required whenever the air outside stands above forty degrees, and a closed light is permitted below that figure only where the frame is matted. Entry in the frame book is required for every closing made out of the daily order, with the reading that occasioned it.

text_narrative: They still talk in the parish about the hotbed the smith made the year the fair was moved. Four feet of stable dung and a foot of loam on top, and he had cucumbers on the table a month before the manor did. What nobody mentions is the second bed, made the same way from the same yard, which went cold in a week and grew nothing but a crop of ink-caps.
text_nonnarrative: Peak temperature in a fermenting bed was roughly proportional to the cube of its linear dimension, so that a bed of four feet held heat some eight times as long as one of two. The constant was a property of the material rather than of the season. Beyond about six feet the relation failed, since the interior was anaerobic and the yield of heat per unit of dung was much lower.

text_narrative: The glasses came with the house, forty of them, and Ruta used them as they were meant to be. Under the first she raised lettuce in February. Under the ninth, set over bare ground by mistake, she found a print of a hand on the inside of the glass. She set it over bare ground again the next night, and again in the week after, and the print came back each time, smaller.
text_nonnarrative: Bell glass: the older pattern, blown in one piece with a knob at the crown, and standing without support. Handlight: a square glazed frame of the same purpose, made in four panes and a lid. Continuous cloche: a run of glasses in a rigid frame, open at both ends of the run and closed by a pane set on edge. Bare cloching: the same equipment over ground with no crop under it.

text_narrative: The shed behind the reservoir still has its bins, six of them, labelled in a hand nobody alive can read. Teilo turns over the third with a trowel and finds it dry to the bottom and full of grit. The fourth is loam, or was, and holds together in a ball when he squeezes it. He mixes the two by eye at three to one, fills nine pots, and sets them along the sill where the glass is thickest.
text_nonnarrative: Four mixtures were held in the standard series, of which the seed compost was the leanest and the potting compost of the third size the richest. Loam made up two parts of the seed mixture and seven of the heaviest potting mixture. Grit was constant at one part throughout. Leaf mould appeared in the two intermediate mixtures only, and lime in none of the four. Each was named for its use and not for its content.

text_narrative: Two years, the book says, and the book has never had to make a heap in a garden nine feet wide. The wire cage takes the whole of the corner where the rhubarb wants to be. Still, the leaves have to go somewhere, and burning them is out of the question with washing out next door on a dry day. Kestrel forks the top layer down and decides not to turn the rest until the frost has been at it.
text_nonnarrative: Leaf mould is worth less as a food than as a structure, and the complaint that a heap gives nothing back to the soil mistakes the second for the first. Its value lies in what it does to the pore space of a heavy soil, which no dressing of fertiliser reproduces. Turning the heap is said to halve the time. It does, and the mould is coarser for it, so the saving is a real one only where the coarseness is no objection.

text_narrative: In the fourth season of the avenue planting, a gale off the estuary loosened sixty of the young limes at the collar. The contractor had staked to two-thirds of the stem height throughout, against the schedule, which called for one-third. Sixty holes were found open at the base, each the width of a fist, and water standing in them. The trees were refirmed and the stakes cut down in the following month.
text_nonnarrative: Wind rock means, in this schedule, any opening at the collar wide enough to admit water, whether or not the stem is displaced. Where a stake stands above one-third of the stem height, the tree is deemed unstaked for the purpose of a claim. Nothing in this clause affects the liability of a contractor for the stake itself. A tree refirmed within the season is not a defective tree.

text_narrative: When the wasps were still owed a debt by the oaks, each wasp was given a room and the oak was made to build it. The grub lay at the centre in a hard cell, and around the cell the oak laid nine layers of its own flesh, and around those a rind. The wasps forgot the debt in time. The oaks did not, and they built the rooms thicker every age, and left no door.
text_nonnarrative: At the middle of a mature gall stood the larval chamber, a cavity lined with a hard shell of a single layer. Outside the shell lay a zone of nutritive tissue, thin and pale, and outside that the bulk of the gall in soft parenchyma. The rind was the outermost part and bore the tannins. An exit canal was absent in the unemerged gall and present as a clean bore in the rest.

text_narrative: Over one summer the foreman of the walled garden lost three crops to the same bloom and named none of them. In June it was the apple at the west end, grey on the young shoots only. In July the gooseberries went, fruit and all, under a felt that rubbed off on a thumb. In August it took the marrow leaves from the edge inward, and the fruit under them swelled as usual and tasted of nothing.
text_nonnarrative: An outbreak is classed by the tissue it occupies and never by the crop. Bloom on young shoots is one class; bloom on the fruit is a second, and the two are held apart even where both are on one apple. Grey felt that rubs off under a thumb is diagnostic of neither. Leaves taken from the edge inward count with the shoots, and loss of flavour in a marrow is no part of the grading at all.

text_narrative: Anyone who parks under the limes on the square knows what comes down in July, and there is an argument about it that has run for twenty years. Half the street calls it sap and half calls it rain off the leaves. The old woman at the corner house says it is neither, that the trees are paying something back, and she leaves a saucer out under the worst branch every night of the month.
text_nonnarrative: Whether honeydew counted as an excretion or as a food was less a matter of chemistry than of which end of the relation was taken as primary. Treated as waste, it belonged to the aphid and its presence on the leaf below was incidental. Treated as payment, it belonged to the ant, and the aphid was a herd. Neither account explained the sooty mould, which was a third party to a bargain it had no share in making.

text_narrative: A surveyor's report on the old bonded warehouse is filed in the morning and withdrawn the same afternoon. The report finds the south gable sound under nine inches of ivy and recommends nothing. The withdrawal notice gives no reason. What the file does contain, on a loose sheet, is a photograph of the gable with the ivy stripped from a strip a yard wide, and mortar missing to the depth of a finger.
text_nonnarrative: Ivy on masonry was blamed for damage it was seldom the author of, and the blame rested on a confusion between adhesion and penetration. The rootlets held to a surface by a secretion and penetrated nothing that was not open. Sound mortar was therefore in no danger from them. That said, a wall under ivy could not be inspected, and the cover was worth more to a bad wall than to a good one.

text_narrative: There were two sisters in a village under the downs who were left a sack of bulbs and no instruction. The elder planted hers at a hand's depth and had one flower from each for nine years. The younger planted hers shallow, a thumb under the grass, and had a great many flowers the first year and none at all the fourth, and a mat of small white bulbs under the turf instead.
text_nonnarrative: Offset production per parent bulb is higher the shallower the planting, and the increase is closer to inverse-square than to linear over the usual range. Flower size runs the other way against the same variable. The two relations cross at about three times the height of the bulb, which is the depth at which neither yield is at its maximum and both are near it. Below six inches the relation is unreliable.

text_narrative: In the third year after the enclosure award, the cutting of the common meadow was set back a fortnight by the vestry and the dispute went to the quarter sessions. Two tenants had cut on the old date and carried the hay before the notice was read out. The court held the notice good and the hay theirs, and ordered the date entered in the parish book, where it stood for sixty years unaltered.
text_nonnarrative: Meadow, in this article, meant land shut for hay and not land grazed in the same season, whatever its herbage. A cutting date entered in the parish book bound every tenant with a share in the ground, and a share was defined by the doles and not by the acreage. Where a date coincided with a day of rest, the day following was the date. Nothing in the article touched the aftermath.

text_narrative: A parish walk to count the hedges was completed in one day in the second week of the month, with eleven walkers on six miles of boundary. The count on the lane hedges ran between four and seven woody kinds in a thirty-yard stretch. On the field boundary behind the pumping station the same stretch gave eleven, and the walkers went over it twice before entering the figure.
text_nonnarrative: Counts on adjacent stretches of one boundary differ by as much as counts on boundaries in different parishes. The mean over lane hedges is five woody kinds to the thirty-yard stretch, with most of the spread accounted for by the presence or absence of a single climber. Observer variance is small on the woody kinds and large on the ground flora, which is why the ground flora is excluded.

text_narrative: Halfway up the ridge the tape runs out before it meets itself and Odger has to mark the bark with chalk and start again from the mark. The trunk leans across the slope, so breast height on the upper side is two feet below breast height on the lower. He takes both, writes both down, and adds a note about the burr at four feet that the tape has had to ride over.
text_nonnarrative: A girth was rejected on the position of the tape and not on the manner of reading it. On a slope, breast height was taken on the upper side alone; a figure read on the lower side was out of class however carefully the tape was held. A burr under the tape was disqualifying whatever its size, and chalk on the bark bore on the record and never on the girth itself.

text_narrative: In the age when trees could still be persuaded, the makers went out with knives and taught two woods to be one. A long slope was cut on each, and a tongue raised in the face of each slope, and the tongues were slid past one another until neither could be drawn out. What the makers could not teach was the joining itself. That the trees did in the dark under the wax.
text_nonnarrative: Each half of the union bears a sloping face and a single tongue cut back into that face at about a third of its length from the upper end. The tongues are reciprocal, one raised toward the tip and the other toward the base, and interlock without any fastening. Cambium is continuous across the joint only along the two long edges. A third tongue is absent in every form of the union.

text_narrative: Nobody in that orchard would ring a tree after the middle of the month, and the reason given was never the sap. The story was about a grower two valleys over who took a half-inch band off a pear in the wrong week and hung the strip of bark on a nail in his shed. The tree bore heavily for one season. The strip, they said, was still green on the nail nine years later.
text_nonnarrative: A complete ring was not a permitted position on any stem carrying the whole of a tree, and a band wider than half an inch was not permitted anywhere. Bark taken from a branch ringed in the same year had no standing. A tree bearing on spurs alone was outside the rule entirely, since the position it forbade could not arise on such a tree. Grafted stems counted as one stem throughout.

text_narrative: Nine hundred feet of ridge and the vent gear answers on eight hundred of it. The rest is the western span, where the rack has been off its pinion since before the handover and nobody has costed the repair. Vaska stands under it with the lamp. Hot air has to go somewhere, and it is going out through the broken pane at the gable, which is why the span nearest the door is the coldest in the house.
text_nonnarrative: The house lay on an east-west axis with a single ridge some nine hundred feet long. Ventilators sat in a continuous run along the southern pitch and in short banks of three along the northern. Below the ridge the roof was of nine-inch panes in a lead frame, and the western gable was blind. The floor stood four feet under the outside ground at the eastern end and level with it at the western end.

text_narrative: In the seventh year of the new planting, the sward between the rows was let to a grazier for the first time and the arrangement lasted one season. Sheep took the bark off nineteen trees below the guards. The account for that year records the loss, the cost of nineteen new guards, and a scythe bought in the autumn. The sward was mown by hand for the eleven years following.
text_nonnarrative: Five kinds of ground cover are found under standard trees, of which close-mown grass is by far the commonest and bare tilth the rarest. Herbal leys hold a middle place, being sown to three species in the ordinary mixture and to nine in the richer. Guards are of two patterns, wire spiral and slatted timber, the second being the only one proof against sheep. Nothing in the list is proof against rabbits.

text_narrative: There was a basketmaker on the flats who would cut no rod that had been left three winters, and the other makers laughed at her for it. Her baskets went to market and came back empty; theirs came back full. In the year the water stood late over the beds, only the young rods were fit to cut, and every maker on the flats worked from her stools and paid her in salt.
text_nonnarrative: Rod quality was habitually judged by colour, which was the least reliable of the indications available and the easiest to fake by steaming. Uniformity of taper mattered more and was harder to see. The trade held that a bed declined after its twentieth year, a claim that rested on no comparison worth the name, since the beds that lasted were the ones cut hardest and the two causes were never told apart.

text_narrative: The first planting on the open ground was made of two peoples, and only one was meant to stay. The quick trees went in between the slow ones and grew over them and kept the wind off their heads for thirty years. Then the axes came for the quick trees, as had been agreed before either was sown. The slow trees have never spoken of it, and they stand in rows to this day.
text_nonnarrative: Calling a nurse row part of the crop or part of the site is not a quibble, since the two answers make different things into failures. On the first account, a nurse that outlives its term is a crop tree in the wrong place. On the second, it is a condition that has failed to lapse, and no tree. What hangs on the choice is whether the belt can be said to have a single age.

text_narrative: Every spring the bed by the gate gives Anka the same argument in a different form. In the first year it is one shoot from below the knuckle, seven feet of it, with nine leaflets to a leaf instead of five. In the third it is four shoots and the named rose down to a stub. In the fifth the bed is all briar and she has stopped calling it the rose bed.
text_nonnarrative: Knuckle: the swelling at the base of a budded rose, where the named wood meets the stock. Sucker: any shoot arising below that swelling, whatever its vigour. Briar: the stock itself, considered as a plant in its own right rather than as a base. Reversion: the condition of a bed in which the briar holds the ground and the named wood does not. Blind wood: a shoot of either kind that bears no flower.

text_narrative: Long before the towers, the keepers of the small trees held that a tree in a tray was a promise and not a possession. Each spring they lifted the tree out, cut a third of the root away, and set it back in the same earth. The tree owed them nothing for it. What it owed, they said, was owed to the tray, which had agreed to be small so that the tree need not.
text_nonnarrative: Most writing on the tray trees was writing about age, and it mistook the sign for the thing: a trunk thickened by fifty years of confinement looked old, and a trunk thickened by feeding looked older still. The honest work in the tradition was in the roots, where nothing showed and no credit was to be had. Its best practitioners were the ones whose trees looked unremarkable in the third decade and plain in the fifth.

text_narrative: A finch and a miller once fell out over a heap of chaff, and the dispute was put to the sieve. Three screens were set in a frame, coarse over fine, and the heap was worked through all three. The miller took what stayed on the top screen and the finch took what fell through the bottom. Neither had thought about the middle, and the middle was where the seed was.
text_nonnarrative: Purity of a lot and cleanness of a lot diverge under any definition of either. Purity is a ratio within the seed itself and takes no notice of what else is in the bag; cleanness is a statement about everything that is not seed. A screen acts on size, so it can raise the second without touching the first. Only a difference in density distinguishes a full seed from an empty one.
